title: Shiva: Meaning and Context
excerpt: Shiva is a major Hindu deity associated with asceticism, destruction, and yoga. The name is not a generic word for consciousness.

quick_answer.question: What does Shiva mean?
quick_answer.answer: Shiva is a principal Hindu god, worshiped in many forms. Some yogic and tantric texts also use Shaiva theology. The name is not a synonym for a private state of mind.

intro: Shiva is a god. In Shaiva traditions he is ultimate in a theological sense. In a studio he is sometimes reduced to a mood of detachment.

sections.heading: What does Shiva mean?
sections.content:
Stories, temples, and philosophical schools do not agree on one portrait. Shakti is often paired with him as power. Tantric practice may be Shaiva without being the same as a yoga class that chants his name once.

The neighboring page is [the shakti entry](/glossary/shakti/). Treat that link as part of the argument, not as decoration.

sections.heading: Where does the word come from?
sections.content:
Britannica's article is a better start than a tattoo glossary. Yoga's historical ties to Shaiva milieus are real and are not a claim that every posture sequence is worship.

A wider map lives at the [ancient wisdom topic](/topics/ancient-wisdom/). Dates and school names matter, because a recent American presentation is often described as if it had no date.

sections.heading: How is the word misused?
sections.content:
If you chant a name, know that you are using a divine name. If you are only reading, keep the theology distinct from a breathing exercise. Do not treat the god as a personality type.

If you want a narrower practical or comparative page, use [the tantra entry](/glossary/tantra/). You can understand the description without joining a group or buying a course.

sections.heading: What should a careful reader refuse?
sections.content:
Do not use Shiva as a brand of calm masculinity. Do not strip the worship and keep the aesthetic. A deity is not a wellness aesthetic.

Readers in the United States often meet a simpler version of the same idea in a class, an app, or a short video. Name that simpler version instead of pretending it is the whole tradition. Traditional teaching, personal report, and research stay in separate sentences on this site. The [editorial policy](/editorial-policy/) is the rule. The [disclaimer](/disclaimer/) applies whenever a sentence leans toward health, safety, or a promised transformation. The [corrections](/corrections/) page is how to challenge a factual mistake. Name the school, the text, or the century whenever a sentence would otherwise float free of history. A reader may stop at the definition when that is all the question required.

key_takeaways: Shiva is defined here in its traditional or philosophical sense.
Popular English often widens the word until it means a mood.
Longer pages on this site carry the disagreements.

faq.question: Is Shiva a scientific term?
faq.answer: No. Shiva is a religious name. States of attention are a different subject.

faq.question: Where is the longer page?
faq.answer: Read the shakti and tantra entries. The longer linked page carries the rest of the context.
